analysis.one_liner: Delays a new federal overtime pay rule for two years in disaster-declared states.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with no cosponsors in September 2016, it was referred to the Senate HELP committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In May 2016 the Labor Department finalized a rule that roughly doubled the salary threshold below which salaried 'white collar' workers must receive overtime pay, set to take effect December 1, 2016. This bill would have pushed that effective date back two years — to December 2018 — but only in states where the President had declared a major disaster after August 14, 2016 (Louisiana's August 2016 floods qualified). The bill was introduced by Louisiana Senator David Vitter, never gained a cosponsor, and never received a committee hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Small business owners and other employers in disaster-declared states, who would have avoided the cost of raising roughly 12,000 workers' salaries above the new threshold or paying them overtime for two more years. Businesses still recovering from floods or other disasters would have had more time to absorb the change.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have frozen the Labor Department's overtime rule — which roughly doubles the salary level below which salaried workers are guaranteed overtime — until December 1, 2018 in states with recent major disaster declarations.

Employers in those states, including Louisiana businesses hit by the August 2016 floods, would have gained two extra years before they had to either raise exempt employees' salaries to the new threshold or start paying them overtime.

analysis.who_pays: Salaried workers in disaster-declared states who earn between the old and new salary thresholds would have gone two more years without guaranteed overtime pay — working long hours for no extra wage. The rule change they would have received in December 2016 would have been delayed until 2018.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mid-salary salaried workers in those states

drawbacks.text: Workers in affected states would have lost two years of overtime protections they were otherwise scheduled to receive, since the bill targeted the specific states where disasters — and therefore likely economic strain — had already been declared.

Supporters of the underlying rule argued the higher salary threshold had already been reduced in response to business concerns and that employers had been given months of notice before the December 1, 2016 effective date. This good-faith objection and the wage cost to workers are the honest trade-offs of the delay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered genuine relief to businesses recovering from disasters, but its cost fell directly on the salaried workers the overtime rule was designed to help — and only in the states where those workers were most likely to have been hit by the same disasters. It was a narrow, targeted delay rather than a full repeal, but the burden landed on ordinary workers' paychecks.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate's labor committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator David Vitter introduced the bill on September 28, 2016, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors, according to Congress.gov's cosponsor page.
No further action was taken; the bill remained in committee when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Salaried workers in disaster-declared states came out ahead: the overtime rule's December 1, 2016 effective date remained in place for them, because the bill to delay it never moved. Employers who would have benefited from the delay gained nothing from the bill's failure, though the rule's fate was ultimately decided in the courts and by the incoming administration rather than by this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Salaried workers who kept overtime rights

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to delay the overtime rule in disaster-declared states; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Small business employers in disaster-declared states (retail, restaurants, and service firms)
industries.note: The bill would have spared these employers from the Labor Department's higher overtime salary threshold for two years — a gain funded by withholding overtime wages from their mid-salary salaried workers. Because it died, they remain subject to the rule as originally scheduled.

industries.industry: Salaried 'white collar' workers earning between the old and new overtime thresholds in those states
industries.note: Not an industry but the direct beneficiary group: because the bill failed, these workers kept the rule's scheduled December 2016 expansion of overtime eligibility rather than losing it for two years.
